Values below box plots show the estimated fold change in adjusted bee richness relative to tropical islands (Supplementary Table 10).

The relationship between angiosperm and bee richness probably reflects a combination of shared biogeographic drivers, such as area and climate, as well as ecological dependence, although the contribution of these factors cannot be separated here. However, the markedly higher baseline bee richness in Mediterranean-type islands at equivalent angiosperm richness is consistent with the hypothesis that temperature seasonality promotes bee specialization57. Seasonal climates can promote bee specialization through temporal resource partitioning while perhumid tropical systems, despite higher plant richness, may present ecological filters that limit bee diversity. Therefore, capturing more detailed information on the complex networks that wild bees form with native plants, and how they vary with island isolation and reduced colonization events, is crucial for developing more complete models of island biodiversity58,59 (reviewed in ref. 1). Yet recent evidence highlights that flowering plant communities may be reliant on bee pollinators when bee richness is comparatively low60. Consequently, we should not expect a simple, predictable relationship between plant and bee richness across islands of differing biomes, isolation and area.

Our study demonstrates that islands account for a substantial share of global bee diversity, including many species that evolved on islands and are endemic. We find that species richness and endemism are partly disconnected, highlighting that these two metrics capture distinct aspects of insular bee diversity. Richness peaks in mid-latitude, Mediterranean-type islands in the Northern Hemisphere, whereas peak endemism occurs in large tropical islands, with these differences being strongest for oceanic islands. These patterns are further supported by the biome-dependent relationship between angiosperm and bee richness, showing that although floral richness is a strong predictor of bee diversity across islands, it does not fully account for the differences in bee richness observed among biomes. Only a small percentage of island bee species have been assessed for extinction risk29,30, and this risk is probably tied to evolutionary distinctiveness rather than richness55. Therefore, our results suggest that conserving bees on islands requires prioritization of areas of unique evolutionary history, from large continental fragments such as Madagascar to remote oceanic archipelagos like the Hawaiian islands, over species richness alone.

Bees are particularly well suited as a model taxon for studying island biogeographical dynamics. They are pivotal pollinators that are closely linked to plant reproduction and ecosystem functioning22, and represent a taxonomically discrete group with an increasing availability of distributional and phylogenetic data. However, much remains to be explored in understanding the mechanisms behind the patterns of colonization and speciation, and the potential for new discoveries. The increasing availability of molecular phylogenies opens up new research avenues for addressing the evolutionary history of bees27. Combined with detailed distribution and trait data61, these resources make it possible to reconstruct historical patterns of colonization, extinction and speciation on islands. With the baseline established here, we lay the foundation for understanding the colonization, diversification and vulnerability of insect diversity on islands more broadly.

We verified the presence of bees on islands on the basis of information available on Discover Life (https://www.discoverlife.org/) and more detailed and recently updated information, notably, for type locality and collection event data, extracted from source files for that resource21. These expert-vetted lists were filtered for island records and joined with spatial data to align species presence with island identifiers. The checklist data on Discover Life were collected from a variety of sources, including taxonomic revisions, primary species descriptions (including synonyms), verified human observations, and undigitized museum records. To avoid complications from historical boundary changes, species were recorded at the current state or country level. The data are available online as a matrix at the country level, with species-specific details provided for finer geographic scales. For further details on how the checklists were sourced see ref. 4. For islands not clearly associated with a specific country or state/province, additional sources were used to confirm species presence based on the broader political region. We then cross-referenced specimens with island-specific faunal checklists from the published literature; for example, when a species was known only from an archipelago we tried to determine its presence on specific islands within the archipelago. These included studies from Abd al Kuri and Socotra from the Socotra Archipelago65, the Azores including Corvo, Faial, Flores, Graciosa, Pico, Santa Maria, São Jorge, São Miguel and Terceira66, Balearic Islands including Ibiza, Mallorca and Menorca67, Bonaire68, Cabo Verde including Boa Vista, Brava, Sal, Santiago, Santo Antão, São Nicolau and São Vicente69, Cuba and East Grand Bahama70, Fiji52,71, Isla de Juventud72, Juan Fernández Islands73, Madeira Archipelago including Madeira, Porto Santo, and Deserto Grande and Selvagens Islands including Selvagem Grande74 and Madagascar75,76. European island checklists were extracted from the latest checklists for European species from Reverte et al.77 and included Åland islands, Great Britain, Ireland, Iceland, Faroe Islands, Malta, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily, Crete, Cyprus and Isle of Man. We also included validated (Research Grade) iNaturalist records (up to December 2024) for all islands available from the initial checklists. Although these entries provide valuable data, a degree of taxonomic doubt remains, consequently, they have been labelled as uncertain within the final dataset pending further validation. The checklists for the Greek islands of Corfu and Rhodes were expanded with records from Rhodes78,79, Corfu80 and the personal collection of T. J. Wood. Recent additions to Corsica and Sardinia were also added81, as were the latest checklists of the Canary Islands82. Finally, the bee fauna of Tasmania was significantly adjusted due to recent taxonomic work on the Parasphecodes subgenus83. Names were cleaned using the synonym lists from Orr et al.4 and Dorey et al.84. In some cases, it was not possible to separate archipelago-level data into island records and some archipelagos were therefore retained in the dataset (for example, for the Solomon Islands).

To classify non-native species and calculate final island native species richness, we used Russo85 as a baseline, complemented by existing checklist information and expert opinion from J.S.A. Using the checklists, we calculated three measures of wild bee richness and endemism on islands. They included: (1) native species richness, calculated as the total number of unique native species included in the checklist for each island (or archipelago, as the case may be); (2) single-island endemism, calculated as the total number of species on the checklist only known from that island; (3) AE, calculated as the total number of species found only on that archipelago: this includes all SIEs.

Using the above checklists, we extracted a spatially explicit database of islands by matching the names from the checklist to those found in the global islands (greater than 1 km2 in area) database of Sayre et al.63. We extracted a vector shapefile of all islands for which we had any wild bee checklist information. In most cases we endeavoured to associate each checklist with a single island entity. In cases where a single name from the bee database is associated with multiple land masses, we extracted all the landmasses for subsequent calculations (for example, Sao Tome and Principe, Saint Vincent and Grenadines, Wallis and Futuna, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Pierre and Miquelon, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Solomon Islands). Duplicate island names and spatial mismatches were checked manually. Following this we harmonized the island names with the islands included in the Global Inventory of Floras and Traits (GIFT) database and extracted information on island area, isolation (distance to mainland), island category (oceanic, fragment or continental), archipelago and richness of angiosperms from GIFT (for more detail, see ref. 20). Islands in the GIFT database were categorized by geological origin into oceanic (volcanic islands and atolls), continental shelf (land-bridge), and complex origin/continental fragments. Categorizing islands into three discrete types is a necessary simplification. Certain cases, such as the tectonic uplift of Cyprus or continental fragments such as Rhodes, New Caledonia and Seram that underwent periods of total submergence, represent intermediate states where biological isolation was prioritized over strict geological origin. Specifically, a lack of historical land-bridge connections was used to classify islands as oceanic in type. Of the final 305 islands, there were 207 oceanic islands, 25 fragment islands and 73 continental islands (see Supplementary Table 12 for a full breakdown by biome).

Species distribution data for 350,707 vascular plant species across 1,967 islands and 1,010 mainland regions were taken from Schrader et al.9 and then associated with islands for which we have bee species checklists. These data were originally sourced from the GIFT v.3.2 database using the R package GIFT86 and are taxonomically standardized according to the World Checklist of Vascular Plants9,20. In the few cases where we had bee checklist data for an island or archipelago that did not correspond to an island or archipelago in the GIFT database—for example, data aggregated at archipelago level in one but not the other—we calculated area and isolation directly from the aforementioned spatial map of islands63 and island-specific literature was used to determine island category and archipelago.

We incorporated additional island-level environmental information by overlaying our island shapefile with a spatial global shapefile of ecoregions62, which is an update of the original WWF biogeographical regionalization of Olson et al.87. This dataset provides a globally standardized classification of terrestrial ecoregions, biomes and biogeographic realms, and was selected because it offers consistent, GIS-based borders that explicitly include oceanic islands, allowing reproducible assignment of islands based solely on spatial overlap. Although developed as a general terrestrial biodiversity classification rather than for specific taxa, the underlying climatic, floristic and evolutionary discontinuities that define these realms are expected to also be relevant for bees, whose distributions are closely tied to vegetation structure and climatic regimes. Each island was assigned to a terrestrial biome and biogeographic realm using the intersect function from the R package sf (v1.0-2188). Biome classifications were aggregated into broader categories (boreal, desert, Mediterranean, temperate and tropical) for comparative purposes (Supplementary Table 13) and the final selected biome was the dominant biome found on the island. Realm classifications were one of Afrotropic, Australasia, Indomalaya, Nearctic, Neotropic, Oceania and Palaearctic. This allowed for consistent ecological context across islands and facilitated analyses of native bee richness by biome type and realm.

We also calculated additional isolation metrics by computing the edge-to-edge distance (km) from each study island to the nearest landmass across three size classes (>1 km2, >1,000 km2 and >10,000 km2) and the cumulative surrounding land area (km2) within buffers of 10 km, 100 km and 1,000 km around each island. To do this, we combined our global island database with a global continental layer from rnaturalearth v1.0.189. We tested correlations (r > 0.7) among all isolation variables prior to model fitting (Supplementary Fig. 1). We selected distance to the nearest landmass >1,000 km2 and the total land area within the 10 km buffer to represent isolation, alongside distance to mainland (km), in the final set of variables with which we conducted model selection. Climate data were extracted from bioclimatic rasters from the CHELSA v2.190 with a resolution of 30 arcsec. The variables included annual mean temperature (BIO1), temperature seasonality (BIO4; defined as the standard deviation of monthly mean temperatures multiplied by 100), annual precipitation (BIO12), and precipitation seasonality (BIO15; defined as the coefficient of variation of monthly precipitation). Local elevation metrics were extracted for each island using the elevatr package (v0.99.1)91. Climate variables were averaged for each island and elevation was recorded as the elevational range of each island.

To ensure comparability and ecological and biogeographical relevance, we limited our final dataset to islands with a minimum area of 5 km2 and located at least 1 km from the mainland. These thresholds helped to remove islands with high edge effects, and limited habitat heterogeneity, while ensuring a meaningful biogeographical break from the mainland.

To explore global patterns of bee sampling on islands we used the BeeBDC protocol outlined in Dorey et al.84 to extract all global records of bees on islands. Specifically, we downloaded all records of Anthophila from Global Biodiversity Information Facility92, Atlas of Living Australia93 and iDigBio. We corrected synonymous names as above using the synonym lists from Dorey et al.84 and Orr et al.4. As part of the cleaning process the data were subset to only include names of species found in the island checklist dataset, ensuring incorrect records of valid species unlikely to occur on the island were removed. To link bee occurrence records with islands spatially, we reprojected all coordinates to match the island shapefile and performed a spatial join, retaining only records intersecting island polygons defined in the checklist dataset. To ensure consistency between occurrence and checklist data, all species listed in the island checklists were added as supplementary records to the public database, standardizing species richness values across sources. The final dataset comprised 663,189 georeferenced records, which were subsequently used to assess sampling effort and spatial coverage across islands included in the analysis. This dataset was used to calculate a proxy for sampling effort and sampling completeness. To measure sampling completeness we calculated sampling coverage across islands using the Chao & Jost64 method via the coverage function in the iNEXT3D R package (v1.08)94. We used a species/island abundance (count of all occurrences per species per island) matrix of all records to estimate the proportion of the total individuals per island that belong to the observed species, using a non-parametric estimator that accounts for the frequency of rare species (singletons and doubletons). To account for large differences in sampling effort we additionally weighted coverage based on the total number of occurrence records, subsequently referred to as a sample-size-adjusted measure of sampling completeness.

We used the Discover Life global checklist through the BeeBDC tool84 as our baseline source for global bee species richness. To generate an estimate of mainland-only species richness, we excluded all species known to occur on islands by comparing with the above checklists and by removing all island-level records from the global checklist. The global checklist was also used to supplement endemism and island-only species data by filtering out species only recorded on islands from the checklist and cross-referencing with the island dataset. The mainland checklist was also used to test island occurrence patterns to create a binary classification of all species as either occurring or not occurring on islands.

We used the island-level checklists to test the key predictors of species richness on islands. We fit a linear mixed-effects model using the lmer function from the lme4 R package (v1.1-37)95, with native species richness as the response variable. We log10-transformed native species richness after adding 1 to all values to accommodate islands with zero native bee species (n = 4) while preserving them in the analysis.

We constructed a full model including the full set of ecological predictors, and then tested all possible model subsets (dredge function, R package MuMIn v1.48.1196). In all models, log10-transformed island area and a measure of island isolation were retained as fixed effects because these variables represent the core predictions of island biogeography theory. We evaluated three alternative isolation metrics in separate full models: log10-transformed distance to the nearest mainland, log10-transformed distance to the nearest landmass exceeding 1,000 km2, and the surrounding land area in a 10 km buffer around the island.

The full model also included biome (5 categories), elevation range (log10), mean annual temperature (scaled), temperature seasonality (log10), annual precipitation (log10), precipitation seasonality (log10), island type (continental, fragment, or oceanic), and sampling completeness (sample-size-adjusted coverage, log10). We also evaluated an Area × Biome interaction and an Isolation × Biome interaction. We assessed collinearity among predictors using variance inflation factors (VIF; R package car, vif function97); mean annual temperature showed high collinearity with biome and other climate variables across all datasets (VIF > 5), and removing it from the full model brought all remaining predictors below this threshold. We therefore excluded mean annual temperature from the full model. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept in all models to account for spatial non-independence among islands within the same archipelago and to allow baseline species richness to vary among archipelagos98. Models were fit by maximum likelihood and ranked by AICc; models with all three isolation-metric were then pooled into a single ranked set of models. When more than one model was within ΔAICc < 2, we selected the simplest model with the fewest degrees of freedom (Supplementary Table 4). The best-supported model included:

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Isolation)ij + β5 × IslandTypeij + β6 × SamplingCompletenessij + uj + εij

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = number of native bee species observed on island i in archipelago j

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km)

IslandTypeij = island type (continental, fragment, oceanic)

SamplingCompletenessij = sample-size-adjusted coverage

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome

β4 = effect of log10(isolation)β5 = effects of island type

The final model included the interaction between area and biome, indicating that the effect of area on species richness varies among biomes. Island type and sampling completeness were retained as fixed effects. Two island groups for which coverage could not be calculated were dropped from the final model (Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn Islands, n = 303). We quantified variance explained by fixed effects alone using marginal R2 and using conditional R2 for variance explained by both fixed and random effects99. To compare species–area relationship slopes among biomes, we extracted biome-specific slopes and their standard errors from the variance–covariance matrix of fixed effects. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (v1.11.1)101. Model predictions and confidence intervals were generated using the fixed-effects design matrix and visualized using ggplot2 (v3.5.2)102. Finally, we fit the same best model for only oceanic and only continental and fragment islands, specifically to compare ISAR slopes among biomes of different island types.

To explore the predictors of endemic species richness and its relationship with total species richness across islands, we used a model selection approach mirroring our richness analysis. We fit a series of linear mixed-effects models using the lmer function from the R package lme4 (v1.1-37)95. Collinearity among predictors was assessed the same way as for richness and mean annual temperature was also removed from all endemism full models.

We focused on islands supporting at least one single-island endemic (SIE ≥ 1; n = 113 islands). In this subset of islands, all biomes are represented apart from boreal, as the boreal islands harboured no endemics. We used the same model fitting procedure as described for the native richness analysis. All models within ΔAICc < 2 are shown in Supplementary Table 7. The best-supported model included:

log10(Endemism)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(Area)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(Area)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(TemperatureSeasonality)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij

Endemismij = number of single-island endemic bee species observed on island i in archipelago j

TemperatureSeasonalityij = temperature seasonality

Isolationij = distance to nearest landmass >1,000 km2

β3 = interaction between log10(area) and biome

β4 = effect of log10(temperature seasonality)

To assess the generality of endemism patterns, we repeated analyses on three subsets: (1) oceanic islands only (n = 69), where endemism is more probably driven by neo-endemic evolution rather than the retention of land-bridge palaeo-endemics; (2) endemic-rich islands (SIE > 5% of total richness; n = 96), focusing on systems where endemism is well-established. We also repeated all analyses for AEs (species endemic to entire archipelagos; AE ≥ 1; n = 217) to confirm patterns were robust across endemism definitions (Supplementary Tables 5 and  7). The archipelago-level approach captures archipelago-wide diversification processes while revealing which individual islands within archipelagos are endemism hotspots (see, for example, ref. 48). For the SIE ≥ 1 and oceanic island subsets, the variance of the archipelago random effect was estimated at zero; however, it was kept for consistency across all models.

Additionally, to formally test how the relationship between richness and endemism varies across biomes, we compared three nested models for SIEs and AEs:

where endemism is predicted solely by richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + (1|Archipelago);

where biome adds information beyond richness: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) + Biome + (1|Archipelago); and

where the slope of the effect of richness varies by biome: log10(SIE/AE) ~ log10(Richness) × Biome + (1|Archipelago)

We compared these nested models sequentially using likelihood ratio tests. If including biome as a fixed effect significantly improves model fit, this indicates that islands with similar richness support different baseline levels of endemism depending on biome. If including the interaction between biome and richness improves model fit then the rate at which endemics accumulate with increasing richness also varies across biomes. We then tested for specific differences among biomes using pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means for intercepts and estimated marginal trends for slopes (FDR correction100) using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101.

To assess the extent to which bee diversity tracks angiosperm diversity across islands, we fitted a linear regression model with native bee richness as the response variable and native angiosperm richness and its interaction with biome as the predictors. We additionally included both island area and isolation as covariates to account for confounding geographic effects that influence the richness of both angiosperms and bees. Variance inflation factors indicated low multicollinearity among predictors (all VIFs < 2.4), supporting the inclusion of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation in the same model. We fit the model for the 175 islands for which we had both bee native richness data and reliable angiosperm richness data from the GIFT database20. Archipelago identity was included as a random intercept to account for spatial non-independence of islands within the same archipelago. To include the interaction with biome we removed boreal islands from the analysis as there were too few islands (3) with which to test the interaction.

To (1) compare baseline shifts (intercepts) across biomes against a single baseline and (2) to conduct a likelihood ratio test on the significance of the interaction between biome and angiosperm richness, we additionally fitted a model with and without the angiosperm richness × biome interaction term. The full model with interaction was:

log10(NativeSpeciesRichness)ij = β0 + β1 × log10(AngiospermRichness)ij + β2 × Biomeij + β3 × (log10(AngiospermRichness)ij × Biomeij) + β4 × log10(Area)ij + β5 × log10(Isolation)ij + uj + εij

NativeSpeciesRichnessij = native bee species richness on island i in archipealgo j

AngiospermRichnessij = native angiosperm species richness

Isolationij = distance to nearest mainland (km)

β1 = effect of log10(angiosperm richness)

β3 = interaction between log10(angiosperm richness) and biome

Using the coefficients from this model, we computed an adjusted bee richness for each island by subtracting the centred contributions of angiosperm richness, island area, and isolation from the observed values. This adjustment standardizes the data, showing the bee richness for each island if it had the global average plant richness, land area, and isolation. Finally, we calculated estimated marginal means for each biome using the emmeans package (V1.11.1)101, and performed post hoc pairwise comparisons (FDR correction)100.

All statistical analyses, data manipulation, and visualizations were conducted in R (v4.5.0)103. In addition to the packages already cited; data processing, post hoc tests, and figure formatting were carried out using the following packages: broom.mixed (v0.2.9.6)104, ComplexUpset (v1.3.3)105, corrplot (v0.95)106, cowplot (v1.2.0)107, ggnewscale (v0.5.1)108, ggrepel (v0.9.6)109, ggtext (v0.1.2)110, kableExtra (v1.4.0)111, lmerTest (v3.1-3)112, maps (v3.4.2.1)113, mgcv (v1.9-4)114, multcomp (v1.4-28)115, multcompView (v0.1−10)116, patchwork (v1.3.0)117, performance (v0.13.0)118, scales (v1.4.0)119, scico (v1.5.0)120, tidyverse (v2.0.0)121 and UpSetR (v1.4.1)122.

Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to mainland) and native bee species richness. Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of isolation was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = −0.15, 95% CI = [−0.26, −0.03], t(130.5) = −2.56, p = 0.012). Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Labelled islands are the top 10% most species-rich islands within each biome (values in parentheses show total native bee richness). Solid line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island.

Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. Point colour indicates the proportion of endemic species per island. Sampling completeness is represented by the log10-transformed sample-size-adjusted coverage on each island. The effect of sampling completeness was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.22, 95% CI = [0.13,0.31], t(294.5) = 4.73, p = 3.46 × 10−6). n = 303 islands.

(A) Relationship between island area (log10 km2) and single-island endemic (SIE) species richness for oceanic islands with at least one single-island endemic (n = 69 islands). Solid black line represents fitted mean regression line from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. The effect of area was evaluated using a two-sided t-test with Satterthwaite’s approximation (β = 0.32, 95% CI = [0.22, 0.42], t(69) = 6.23, p = 3.18 × 10−8). Circles are coloured by the proportion of native species that are endemic. (B) Relationship between island isolation (log10 distance to nearest mainland, km) and SIE richness for oceanic islands. Values above zero indicate more SIEs than predicted by richness alone; values below zero indicate fewer. Numbers show the median fold-change relative to model predictions. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test; χ² = 33.18, df = 3, p = 2.95 × 10−7) Table S7); letters denote groups that differ significantly based on two-sided post-hoc pairwise comparisons of estimated marginal means (FDR correction, p < 0.05). Overlaid box plots represent the median (center line) and 25th and 75th percentiles (bounds of box/interquartile range (IQR)); whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values within 1.5×IQR. (C) Relationship between total native species richness (log10) and archipelago endemics (AE; islands with at least one AE, n = 217 islands) richness (log10), coloured by biome. Unlike SIE, the rate at which AE accumulates with richness varied significantly among biomes (likelihood ratio test on the richness × biome interaction; χ2 = 32.25, df = 3, p = 4.63 × 10−7; Table S7). Solid lines represent fitted mean regression lines from mixed-effects model, with dashed lines indicating 95% confidence intervals. (D) Residuals from the AE richness model across biomes (n = 217). Boxplots, violins and letters are the same as in Panel B. Including biome significantly improved model fit (two-sided likelihood ratio test, χ2 = 40.37, df = 3, p = 8.90 × 10−9; Table S7).

#1411. Man City are failing to give their supporters something to stand behind as Enzo Maresca's side radiate uncertainty with meek display in Fulham draw, writes JACK GAUGHAN

Published: 11:04 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 14:16 EST, 21 November 2026

The bananas are disappearing now winter is coming, the fire and fury waning with each passing week. In legal limbo, Manchester City’s supporters need something – anything – to stand behind but increasingly their team refuse to provide that solace.

City were booed off at the end as Enzo Maresca ducked down the tunnel. Some of that could have been directed at referee Thomas Bramall, after Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal, but certainly a significant number were jeering what they’d just seen. That simply does not happen at the Etihad Stadium, even during the torrid run of two years ago.

But they are witnessing a squad who radiate uncertainty. Who take three touches when two will do; who always receive possession squarely facing their own goal; who do not create passing lines for their mates. And crucially, who are forever momentarily confused as to who exactly is picking up which runner and those split seconds make all the difference in this division.

There is just this strange state of unease around how they want to approach games at the moment, something that adversity can provoke and something that Maresca is adamant he can correct. A coach of his calibre should do given the time and freedom.

Yet when he spent the two-week international break studying clips and fashioning ways of improving, he cannot have envisaged a scenario whereby home fans were so incredulous at a lack of energy that they were roused to their feet when Haaland deigned to close down Bernd Leno and force an error.

Man City put in an underwhelming performance as they were held to a 1-1 draw by Fulham

Enzo Maresca's side are radiating uncertainty and look worryingly vulnerable at the back

Rodrigo Muniz made City pay as he put an impressive Fulham 1-0 ahead after 16 minutes

Fulham popped it about nicely and at will. Found pockets to hurt their illustrious hosts, who were again asking a centre half – in this case Marc Guehi – to charge into midfield. City did have more balance than at Nottingham Forest for including Ayyoub Bouaddi for Enzo Fernandez, yet Alvaro Arbeloa still aggressively pressed them in that area to some success.

‘I told the players that we will have the chance to beat them if we play with courage,’ said Arbeloa, who was indebted to the towering performance of defender David Affengruber.

Arsenal will have watched this grinning and could easily be racking up an unassailable lead once these teams meet in north London next Sunday. Unassailable with all the usual caveats about the appeal and what this season may or may not eventually mean.

City did create enough statistically but as with other games of late, that did not tell the whole story.

Calvin Bassey pirouetted through midfield, the heavily derided Gianluigi Donnarumma thwarting a number of strong Fulham chances, and City appeared somewhat lost and out of ideas.

Elliot Anderson equalised with a superb volley but City failed to create much after that

Maresca expressed his concern at City's lack of clean sheets after they struggled again

That is a worrying departure from recent defeats, where they attacked with the same abandon as that early season flourish when they might as well have hosted games at Madison Square Gardens and played with an orange ball.

MAN CITY (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 7; Khusanov 6, Dias 6, Guehi 5, O’Reilly 5 (Gvardiol 78); Anderson 7, Bouaddi 7 (Fernandez 85); Ndiaye 6 (Allan 78), Foden 7 (Cherki 70), Doku 5; Haaland 5

FULHAM (4-2-3-1): Leno 6; Tete 6, Affengruber 8, Bassey 7, Sessegnon 7 (Palacios 83); Berge 6, Charles 7; Bobb 7 (Garcia 78), King 6 (Larsson 70, 6), Iwobi 7 (Robinson 70, 6); Muniz 7 (Cairney 83)

Met with a Fulham who had not conceded more than once in the league since the start of September, City failed to create a meaningful opportunity in the last 25 minutes of a match they were desperate to win and should have been in the ascendancy of after Elliot Anderson’s volleyed equaliser after half time.

Maresca, though, is more concerned with a lack of clean sheets. It’s now none of those in nine games in all competitions for the first time in seven years, with Rodrigo Muniz opening the scoring on 16 minutes. A throw inside Fulham’s own third prompted Guehi to jump and lose his duel, City turned around and Oscar Bobb laid on for Muniz.

‘We’re conceding too many goals,’ Maresca said. ‘We need to avoid it. You need to win games 1-0. You need clean sheets. We’re not able to do it. But I can see many positive aspects. We started four months ago and not four years ago.

‘We’ve conceded almost 80 per cent of our goals at the start of the first half and second half. It’s something we need to improve. It’s a throw in at the corner flag and nobody is expecting they can create something.’

Maresca was also insistent that Haaland ought to have been awarded an equaliser before the break when poking in on the goal line, yet Bramall adjudged that Leno had the ball under control on field, with VAR not overruling.

Some hard luck, some profligacy with Haaland squandering a couple of big chances, but the day was summed up when in stoppage time, Jeremy Doku was penalised for a foul throw.

#1409. Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa

From the moment Ezri Konsa pulled on an Arsenal shirt, he has moved with all the composure of a man who knows exactly where to be and when. The centre-back has required no adaptation period in north London, where he has filled the considerable shoes of William Saliba with such class that Arsenal have hardly missed the Frenchman at all.

The loss of Saliba to a long-term back injury was supposed to be a major problem for Arsenal. Instead, the situation has now reached a point where some fans are wondering how Saliba will get back into the side. That may prove a little extreme, but the fact there is even a discussion is proof of Konsa’s superb impact at the Emirates Stadium.

“Unbelievable,” Mikel Arteta, the Arsenal manager, said of his £55m signing. “He’s come to a huge club and to position yourself in that manner, and to perform at the level he is, it is very difficult to do. We are really lucky to have him.”

In Arsenal’s latest victory, their seventh from eight matches in the Premier League this season, Konsa offered all of his usual defensive security and calmness in possession. Even more excitingly, he also scored his first goal for the club, smashed in from close range after a corner had caused chaos in Everton’s penalty area. It was Arsenal’s first set-piece goal of the season.

“I have been waiting to score my first goal for a while,” Konsa said. “I spoke to the set-piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well. We felt as players that it was coming, and today was the day.”

Some eyebrows were raised when Arsenal paid such a large fee to sign Konsa from Aston Villa. The Villa fans, though, were not among those who questioned the price or the player’s ability. They have known for years at Villa Park that Konsa is a player of the highest quality, and they will not be surprised by his exceptional start to his Arsenal career.

The same is true of the Arsenal players. Arteta asked the England internationals in his squad about Konsa before buying him, and the feedback was overwhelmingly positive. Konsa was already close friends with Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Eberechi Eze before completing his transfer from Villa.

Konsa’s start to life at Arsenal is all the more impressive because he did not even have a pre-season. He effectively came straight from the World Cup into the club, and has been starting games since early September. His first start was against Chelsea, when he endeared himself to the home fans with a crunching tackle on former team-mate Morgan Rogers.

Konsa, 29, has quickly built a strong relationship with Gabriel Magalhães, his defensive partner who scored Arsenal’s other goal here against Everton, from Ben White’s cross. For both centre-backs to find the net felt like a throwback to last year, when Arsenal were so dangerous from crosses, and underlined how Arteta’s team are capable of hurting their opponents in many different ways.

The nature of the goals might give a misleading impression of Arsenal’s performance, though. This was not a gritty win. Arteta’s side produced some excellent passing moves and circulated the ball with menace throughout the game. They were also a little open at times, especially in the first half when Everton created a handful of decent chances.

Thierno Barry missed the best of those opportunities, with the score at 1-0. It was the closest the visitors came to hurting the champions, aside from some of James Tarkowski’s full-blooded tackles. “I felt we didn’t really get to a level that was good enough to get near them,” admitted David Moyes, the Everton manager.

The victory, combined with Manchester City’s defeat earlier in the day, put Arsenal level on points at the top of the table. Aside from the extraordinary thrashing at Brighton, Arteta’s side have looked just as solid, if not more so, than last season. That speaks volumes of the quality in the team, of course, but also says plenty about the way Konsa has adjusted to his new surroundings. Thanks to him, Saliba’s absence has not hurt at all.

“Great feeling, it always is. A clean sheet, a goal – my first goal for the club – so a fantastic day overall.

“I’ve been waiting to score my first goal for a while. I spoke to the set piece coach before the game and he told me he’s been waiting for my goal as well, so it was only right that I got the goal today.

“I’ve come to this stadium for many seasons, I know how tough it is to play against us. It’s not surprising to me.

“We are champions and to be champions you’ve got to win games consistently. This is our home and we want to win as many games here as possible.”

All over at the Emirates and the champions go level on points with Manchester City at the top of the table.

They kept another clean sheet and scored from a set-piece again. All is right in Arsenal’s world!

Oscar Bobb’s first Premier League goal for Fulham earned a 1-0 win over Coventry that lifted the Cottagers clear of the relegation zone.

Bobb produced a fine bit of individual skill to strike in the 80th minute as he twisted his way into the box and bent a shot into the far corner, only his second goal for the club in any competition since his £27million move from Manchester City back in January.

That was enough to give Fulham their first away win in nine attempts, a run that dated back to February, only a week after they ended their winless start to the league campaign by edging out Hull 1-0 as the pressure continues to ease on Alvaro Arbeloa.

Josh King had earlier hit the post for the visitors, who edged Coventry in just about every department to leave Frank Lampard’s side second-bottom of the table.

The hosts had only brief spells of sustained possession in Fulham’s half, but did little to trouble Bernd Leno on a frustrating afternoon which bought the CBS Arena back down to earth after their 4-1 win over Newcastle in their last home outing.

Odegaard drives a shot high over the ball as Arsenal close in on another clean sheet.

Probably sums up Zubimendi’s season so far that he finally gets some meaningful minutes in the Premier League and ends up getting smashed in the face and covered in his own blood. This is after he got injured in a cool-down a few weeks ago. When your luck’s out...

Brilliant play from Oscar Bobb as he cuts inside on his left foot and bends a shot into the far bottom corner for the away side.

Treatment is needed for Zubimendi after he is caught on the nose by Barry.

Big chance for Everton. Garner whips a teasing cross into the box, Dewsbury-Hall meets it with his head on the run but the ball flies just wide of the post.

EvertonOFF Johnson, Mykolenko ON Dibling, Hackney

Tarkowski is the latest yellow card for Everton after a foul on Havertz.

Eze with a poor cross into the box. He fails to run back quickly and Arteta sprints to the edge of the touchline and goes berserk at the midfielder.

How have Arsenal reacted to their top scorer Saka being injured? Both of their centre backs have scored for the first time this season.

On his 200 Premier League appearance for Arsenal, Gabriel marks it with his first goal of the season.

It is a lovely move with slick one-touch passing. The ball is fed to White making a run down the outside and he clips the ball to the far post for Gabriel to head home.

OFF Merino, Lewis-Skelly, GyokeresON Calafiori, Guimaraes, Havertz

Garner is booked for Everton now after barging into Merino off the ball.

Arteta is shown a yellow card for something. Not sure what for yet. But the Arsenal manager is looking to make some changes off the bench.

Arsenal have been guilty of overplaying today. Opting for the extra pass rather than taking a shot. The game is open at the moment and that makes things dangerous for the home side.

Yellow card for Lewis-Skelly after bringing down Johnson. Gabriel is back on the pitch and seems happy enough to continue.

Arsenal have defensive options in Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori and Mosquera if Arteta wants to avoid taking any risks.

A worry for Arsenal as Gabriel jars his knee into the ground as he tries to clear the ball. The Brazilian is receiving treatment and hobbles off the pitch.

Gabriel immediately raised his hand for medical attention after making that clearance. He really extended his leg to get the ball away. Looks to be in a lot of pain.

Latest corner from Arsenal after Eze’s shot is blocked by Rohl. Rice’s delivery into the near post is headed clear to Odegaard, who shoots ambitiously from distance and Pickford collects the ball comfortably.

Arsenal get the match restarted. The longer the match goes on without extending the lead, Everton will think they have a chance.

Before today, Arsenal had averaged five corners per match in the Premier League this season. In the first 45 minutes here, they had 10 corners.

Yellow card for Mykolenko after he catches White wide on the right. Rice whips the ball in and Merino meets it with a flick goalwards but the ball goes over the bar.

That is the final touch of the half and the players are running off to get dry!

Big chance for Everton. White thinks he has time when he heads the ball back to Raya but he does not connect well and Barry is there to pick it up and he flicks a shot at goal but Raya reacts quickly to parry the ball.

Raya is penalised for taking too long with the ball and Everton have a cheap corner. Danger is cleared by Arsenal as they force Everton back into their half.

The conditions are terrible at the moment. Heavy wind and rain causing havoc.

A lot of set-pieces for Arsenal today as they continue to put Everton under the cosh. Can they take advantage of their dominance again before the break?

Arsenal have found their groove again, with Madueke twice going close to extending their lead. Rice, Lewis-Skelly, Odegaard and Merino are forming a box in midfield and Everton don’t seem to know how to shut them down.

Another effort at goal for Madueke. This one is a snapshot from the edge of the box that goes into the side netting.

Madueke should do better. Rice finds him and the winger drives into the box. He takes a shot but drags a right-footed effort wide.

Chance for Arsenal. Rice finds space behind the Everton midfield and drives forward. He plays a pass to Lewis-Skelly, who lays it off to Eze. The England midfielder sidefoots a cross into the box but no one in an Arsenal shirt is there to meet it.

Courtesy of Opta: Arsenal scored their first set-piece goal in all competitions (not including penalties) since May of last season against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one.

George is looking lively for Everton. He tries to come inside and whip an effort to the far corner but the ball deflects wide.

From the corner, Gabriel clears off the line after Raya loses track of the ball.

Everton have responded impressively to the Konsa goal and have been the better team since falling behind. Midfielders Garner and Armstrong are growing into the game quite nicely.

Everton have responded well to going behind here. The early goal against them will have ripped up any plans to sit deep and play on the counter.

Set-pieces are back on the menu for Arsenal. Ezri Konsa’s first goal for the club is their first goal from a corner this season, which will come as a relief to set-piece coach Nicolas Jover. “Set piece again, ole ole,” sing the Arsenal fans. Arteta’s side had started the game on the front foot.

Arsenal had not scored from a corner this season... until now. Konsa breaks the deadlock after a melee in the box and his pokes the ball into the net.

A couple of early set pieces from Declan Rice. Everton do well to clear the danger. But have another one now...

Horrible conditions at the Emirates today. The rain has been lashing down. The Emirates drainage system is usually able to cope with this sort of thing. If the wind picks up, that’s likely to be a bigger problem for the two teams.

After a minute’s applause in honour of Ken Friar, the match makes a prompt start at the Emirates.

“Yeah, we’ve had a good start. Obviously, we had a bit of a blip last week against Chelsea. I don’t think we, as a team, won first and second balls enough and that’s something the manager wants us to get back to today. You’ve got to win your battles.”

On what makes Arsenal difficult to play...

“They’re reigning Premier League champions, a top side that has been knocking on the door to win the title for a few years before as well. They’re a team at a high level but this is what Premier League football is all about and it’s up to us to get a result.”

“Well, we play every two-and-a-half days so we didn’t have much time to recover, so we need full energy. There are certain specific players as well that they fit really well for the game that we expect today and that’s how we start.”

“A very competitive team, a really well organised team. I think that it’s very clear what they want to do, where they want to take the game. The threats, when they have a space to run, any time that they are able to put the ball in their box, you know the presence and aggression that they have. So, yeah, we have to really be at it and be very aggressive from the beginning.”

One of the clearest signs a football club is in a good place is when the debate switches from whether the team are winning to how they are winning.

This is currently Arsenal and Mikel Arteta’s world. For years, Arsenal coaches and players were asked how and when they would start collecting major trophies again. With no concern about their capacity to challenge for top honours over the coming years, the style has become the main focus.

It’s a welcome “problem” – or some might argue a non-existent one – for Arteta while his side is so strong. Building a fortress is the expensive, time-consuming and difficult part. Once it’s constructed and established, how you decorate it is a matter of taste.

Whether neutrals will hold the current champions in the same regard as the great Arsène Wenger sides will be a trivial concern if Arteta does what no Arsenal manager has since 1935 – defend the league title – and then add a few more, which is a serious possibility based on the balance of power in England and the likely punishment heading Manchester City’s way.

Today there will be tributes to Ken Friar, who passed away at the age of 92 earlier this year. Advertising boards outside the Emirates Stadium have been taken over by images of Friar, who had a remarkable 70-year association with the club.

In today’s programme, captain Martin Odegaard has written the following: “It’s exceptional people like Ken Friar who have built the club into what it is today, and we as the current team are the ones privileged to continue his legacy.”

This is a first Premier League start of the season for Viktor Gyokeres, who has been behind Kai Havertz in the pecking order over the past few months. Gyokeres has yet to score in nine appearances in all competitions this season, although he would (understandably) make the point that it’s harder to do so when you are coming off the bench late in games.

For Arsenal, Arteta shuffles his team after the draw against Bayern: White, Lewis-Skelly, Merino, Eze and Gyokeres start.

Max Dowman, who scored a memorable goal in this fixture last season, is on the bench.

For Everton, Jack Grealish misses today’s game due to sickness, while Jarrad Branthwaite is absent because of concussion protocols despite finishing last week’s match with Chelsea after a head collision with Emi Martinez.

Arsenal: Raya, White, Gabriel, Konsa, Lewis-Skelly, Rice, Merino, Odegaard, Madueke, Eze, Gyokeres.Subs: Arrizabalaga, Timber, Hincapie, Calafiori, Mosquera, Zubimendi, Guimaraes, Dowman, Havertz

Everton: Pickford, Tarkowski, O’Brien, Armstrong, Rohl, Dewsbury-Hall, George, Barry, Garner, Mykolenko, JohnsonSubs: Travers, King, Maitland-Niles, Keane, Dibling, Norgaard, Alcaraz, Hackney, Braiden Graham

Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

#1408. Formidable and relentless Bournemouth's astonishing form is no mere hot streak, writes JAMES SHARPE, as dominant Cherries beat Forest to claim NINTH win in a row

Published: 12:38 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 14:28 EST, 21 November 2026

This is all becoming rather inevitable at Bournemouth. Will they ever stop winning? Will Evanilson ever stop scoring?

The numbers alone are astonishing. Nine wins on the bounce for the first time in their history, their victory here against Nottingham Forest making it six on the spin at home at an aggregate score of 15 to nil. Five wins in a row in the Premier League for the first time, too, a result that moved them into the top four.

This is Bournemouth, remember. Only this is Bournemouth now.

Make no mistake: this is no hot streak. This is not a team under Marco Rose carried to win after win after win on a wave of momentum and vibes. This is relentless, breathtaking stuff. This is a team that, week after week, outplays every team that stands in front of them. It doesn’t matter if it’s Forest, or Manchester United, or AC Milan. Bournemouth turn up and they blow their opponents away.

They move it quicker and sharper, they win it back faster and higher. They give teams no time to think or breathe, so it’s little wonder they have no answer.

‘We never really struggled, said Rose. 'We suffered a little bit at the end, but we defended quite well together, and that's why it's a deserved win.

Bournemouth racked up their sixth successive league victory and ninth in all competitions

'If we use the right approach every game – and this is really, really demanding – we win games. Next game, we have to prove it again. If we do it, then we can keep the level up. But as I said, this is a tough job.

‘The collective is strong, but even this we have to maintain. Because if you win games…I mean, some of our players right now are in a lot of noise and rumours.

'If we are able to keep these kinds of things away from the locker room, and if everyone comes into training every day, works hard and gives everything for the club and the team, then we are really, really good.'

The only real surprise was that Evanilson, Bournemouth’s talismanic Brazilian, didn’t leave with more than just his one, now customary, goal.

That itself was another fine finish after Tyler Adams won the ball high up the pitch – obviously – dinked it across to James Hill, back after his first England call-up, who flicked a header into Evanilson’s path. He thumped it past Matz Sels to do the rest.

Rose, who called him a ‘real No9’ the other week, had been urging him to get into the box more to finish off chances. He did that, all right. Twice earlier in the game, he raced on to through balls only to be denied by Sels and a last-ditch tackle from Jair Cunha.

His opening strike, his eighth goal in his last nine games, means he is the first Premier League player to reach double figures for goal contributions with six goals alongside his four other assists. He leads the press, he creates chances, he scores goals. He does the lot.

That’s now six league games in a row he’s found the net, halfway to breaking Jamie Vardy’s record of 11 in a row. You wouldn’t put it past him.

Bournemouth’s talismanic Brazilian Evanilson scored for the sixth successive league match

Forest came into this, after all, off the back of a huge, much-needed victory against Manchester City. After just one win in Oliver Glasner’s opening nine league games, that was the performance those around Forest felt that could spark the season into life.

It was also meant to be the one where Liam Delap’s Forest career burst into life with two thunderous goals in a bullying, battering-ram showing.

Alas, they both ran into a proper team this week.

Forest tried to go direct to Delap, partly to try to bypass the intense Bournemouth press, but nothing stuck. Delap lost possession with 23 of his 39 touches. He committed more fouls than he had shots and found his way into the referee’s book for clumsily bundling over Adam Smith.

The visitors huffed and puffed in the second half but never really looked like scoring. The closest they got was a couple of speculative long-range efforts from Morgan Gibbs-White and James McAtee before a late goalmouth scramble nearly provided an opening through chaos more than creativity.

It was only the busy hands of Sels that kept the scoring respectable.

’The defeat was deserved,’ said Glasner. ‘City and today were completely different. It's like a different sport. This is football, but it's different.

'When teams play like City, when it's more of a tactical game, we are doing well. When it's more of a physical, intense game, we're struggling. Today our weaknesses came to the surface.’

When asked if he had the players to play this way, Glasner responded: 'Right now, I have to say no. If not, we will add players. If we believe we need somebody to add this physicality, these quick solutions, we will do it.'

Did they expect much else, though? Forest never beat Bournemouth. That’s 13 meetings in a row now they have failed to win.

‘Nottingham Forest, it’s happened again,’ sang the home fans in the final few minutes.

Liam Delap and Nottingham Forest crashed into a proper team as they came back down to earth after their win over Man City before the international break

Marcus Tavernier's performances could get a chance with England if he maintains his form

Bournemouth have already had a couple of deserved England call-ups this season in Hill and midfielder Alex Scott. How long until Marcus Tavernier gets his chance?

No English player has scored more Premier League goals this season than the Bournemouth winger, level with Morgan Rogers and Dominic Calvert-Lewin, and once again he was at the heart of everything good the Cherries do.

His superb cross behind the Forest defence found Justin Kluivert for Bournemouth’s second of the afternoon. He danced through the Forest defence to set up Rayan for a late chance.

'It was my 11th Premier League game today, and I couldn't see better offensive midfielders so far this season,’ said Rose.

‘If you see how he works and how he plays, the quality he has, he scores goals. He's 27, he's at the best age.

‘If he plays well, if he stays healthy, I think, like with Hilly, these things come. They're just around the corner.'

#1407. Why Everton School Visits Are Making A Mark

“Captain Underpants”. The laughter that follows is infectious. It seems doubtful that it was an honest answer to the question posed to Zach Lee by the young boy located somewhere near the front of the classroom: “What is your favourite book?” But it got exactly the reaction he was after.

The room is abuzz. It has been for much of the past hour.

Goalkeeper Lee and five of his Everton Under-21s teammates have gleefully taken up the task of being reading buddies to the children of Ellesmere Port’s Meadow Primary School, one of six schools that make up the recently renamed Everton Multi-Academy Trust (EMAT). Seven miles away, six of their Under-21 peers are doing likewise at Oldfield Primary School in Chester.

Nearer to Liverpool, the hollers that greeted Everton Women’s Holly McNamara and Karen Holmgaard 24 hours earlier are still reverberating around the corridors of Bidston Avenue Primary School.

Christian Nørgaard and close friends Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George are also familiar with the noise the pupils at the Birkenhead school can make. Last month, the trio were serenaded with a ukulele rendition of Spirit of the Blues on a visit there. Blue ukuleles, of course.

If the colour of the musical instruments is a cute indicator of the strengthening ties between the football club and the EMAT schools, the time being spared by the players is of much greater significance.

It is intended to demonstrate a cross-Club connection with EMAT, which sits alongside Everton in the Community as one of Everton’s associated organisations. “Part of the Everton family,” as Everton’s Chief Tax and Sustainability Officer and Chair of Trustees for EMAT Alison Haynes puts it.

But there is a deeper intention, too. “We want to use the power of the Everton crest to inspire and engage youngsters in education,” says Steven Baker OBE, CEO of EMAT. Baker has seen this in evidence for more than a decade, having previously served as Principal of Everton Alternative Provision Free School, the award-winning L4 facility that offers youngsters who have struggled in mainstream schools a route back into education.

Lee and his Under-21 colleagues, McNamara and Holmgaard are all supporting one particular mission of EMAT - to inspire youngsters towards a life-long love of reading. More immediately, to ensure they have the requisite literacy level to adequately prepare them for what lies ahead in secondary school education.

In Ellesmere Port, Chester and Birkenhead, the players are tackling their role head on. Books - donated by Everton staff to help replenish the schools’ libraries - are strewn across the tables and spilling onto the floor. No-one’s troubled by the mess.

Julia Donaldson’s greatest hits are being played out across the room. Michael Morpurgo – a childhood favourite author of midfielder Jack Patterson – can be heard, too. ‘Bluey’ is an appropriately named hit on another table. And then there’s Lee and a group of little ones giggling at Captain Underpants.

Close by to the classroom at Meadow, Everton’s leading post-war goalscorer Graeme Sharp is here too, continuing the literacy theme by officially opening the school’s newly-refurbished library.

“These children will remember today,” says Baker. “They will remember players from Everton coming into school and taking the time to sit with them.

“They love hearing stories but they also love having someone to read to. Both aspects are so important for a child’s development.”

As is music. It’s why Dibling, George and Norgaard found themselves being taught the chords to one of Goodison’s – and now Hill Dickinson Stadium’s – favourite tunes last month.

Studies show a direct correlation between a child mastering a musical instrument and making their mark in maths and other creative fields.

The Toffees trio left behind gifts of recorders (blue ones), helping the school expand the opportunities it can offer to its pupils.

“We find it’s really important for their resilience and it's good for the children mentally and socially to have the opportunity to not only play an instrument, but to play to an audience,” says Bidston Avenue headteacher Stuart Brady, a Tranmere Rovers fan.

“It's great for us as a school to have the connection we do with Everton and the players. Days like this are great, but it's also about the children feeling they belong to something bigger.”

And the proof that EMAT is getting it right is stacking up. In 2024, Everton Free School and Everton Football College – the two original schools on which the Trust was founded – were jointly awarded an ‘Outstanding’ rating by Ofsted. Earlier this year, the respected national TES Awards named EMAT (then The People’s Learning Trust) as its Trust of the Year for trusts with nine schools or fewer.

With the support of a Premier League football club and its players behind them, it is hoped the collective will continue to go from strength to strength.

The intention is that Everton’s Under-21s will return to the schools to resume their reading buddy duties at junctures throughout the season, strengthening their bonds with the schools and pupils. It is seen as a vital part of the players’ professional development.

Representatives from the Men’s and Women’s team will continue to play their part also. Merlin Röhl has already been a guest of Oldfield Primary School’s after-school chess club, taking up an invitation to share his love of the ancient game with the next generation.

“We understand the responsibility and influence we have as a football club when it comes to our communities,” says Haynes. “And you cannot understate the impact the player visits have.

“The atmosphere and the smiles you see in the room, the energy they give to the children… it’s truly wonderful.”

#1406. An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 659, pages 628–633 (2026) Cite this article

The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars1,2. This is theorized to happen through common envelope evolution (CEE)3, when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag4,5. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, which originates from the CEE of an approximately 7M⊙ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as an approximately 0.7M⊙ companion inspiralling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven-year period of gradual brighteningone of the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. This phase is radiatively efficient, consistent with predictions for convective transport in CEE5,6,7,8. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core powers the ejection of the outermost 10% of the stellar envelope at speeds about 10× the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope4,9,10,11, 0.01 ≲ α ≲ 0.4. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

Optical spectra of the AT 2025abao eruption. Its spectral evolution matches the characteristic evolution seen in LRNe — blue continuum with emission lines at early times that transitions to a red continuum with molecular absorption features at late times.

Near-infrared spectra of AT 2025abao, from its precursor phase (red) and the eruption (blue). The spectra during the precursor phase resemble late M-type stars, while those during the eruption shows a transition to hotter temperatures. Notably, the CO absorption bands are seen in all spectra, indicating that some molecular gas remains intact even after the eruption.

Theoretically calculated dust mass around the quiescent progenitor system as a function of binary mass ratio using analytical prescriptions (black line) and detailed simulations (squares). The black shaded region marks the range expected by varying stellar parameters in the analytical model (section ‘Comparisons to theoretical predictions of enhanced mass loss’). The observed dust mass from the archival progenitor SED and the JWST observation is shown in purple, which constrains the system mass ratio to \(q=0.1{0}_{-0.08}^{+0.10}\).

Previously identified sources such as V1309Sco, M31-LRN-2015, AT 2019zhd (circles) exhibit a gradual brightening by several magnitudes prior to its eruption. AT 2025abao (stars) differs from these sources, as it only shows a bumpy  ≈ 1 magnitude brightening before transitioning to its eruption.

Evolution of FWHM velocities inferred from our spectra (red), compared to theoretical expectations for momentum-conserving collisions with CBM following a ρ(r) ∝ r−2 density profile (blue solid line). The broken lines indicate the expectation by including an additional mechanical power source, such as a surviving binary, injecting momentum into the ejecta. Our observations constrain the magnitude of this power source \(\mathop{E}\limits^{.}\lesssim 1{0}^{40}\) erg s−1.

LRNe for which progenitor primary stars have been identified are plotted as coloured points, colour-coded by the binding energy of the star. LRNe with no progenitor identifications are plotted as grey points. The eruption of AT 2025abao (star) is remarkably similar to other LRNe, despite having a progenitor with the lowest binding energy ever measured.

a, The quiescent binary system comprising a  ≈ 7 M⊙ AGB and a  ≈ 0.7 M⊙ star, surrounded by an extended dust shell from mass loss from the binary following Roche Lobe overflow of the primary. b, The precursor brightening phase that began in 2018, marking the onset of CEE, powered by frictional drag on the inspiraling companion lasting for  ≈ 7 years. The mass outflow rate during this phase is  ~10−2 M⊙ yr−1, producing  ~0.1 M⊙ of CBM in an equatorial disk around the binary (dark brown). c, The ballistic eruption in late 2025 from the merger of the inspiraling companion with the primary core, resulting in the ejection of  ≈ 0.1 − 0.2 M⊙ of the primary envelope, and sublimation of a large fraction of dust around the binary. d, The eventual lightcurve powered by shock-interactions between freely expanding merger ejecta (indicated by yellow arrows) and equatorially focused CBM. The surviving pre-existing dust is traced by our JWST observations. The black arrows between the panels indicate the progression of time.

#1404. O'Neill hails recalled midfield duo Oxlade-Chamberlain and McCowan after both net to help sink St Mirren

Published: 15:17 EST, 21 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EST, 21 November 2026

Celtic manager Martin O’Neill hailed midfield duo Alex Oxlade-Chamberlain and Luke McCowan after the recalled pair both scored in the 4-1 home win over St Mirren.

With Mika Baur facing 10 weeks out with an ankle injury and Benjamin Nygren nursing a heel problem, O’Neill handed McCowan his second start of the season and Oxlade-Chamberlain his fifth, as the two joined forces for the first time.

Oxlade-Chamberlain and McCowan netted either side of Camilo Duran in a nine-minute flurry of goals late in the first half with Callum McGregor making it four for Celtic in the second period before Killian Phillips reduced the deficit for Saints from the penalty spot.

O’Neill said: ‘Alex has been waiting around for a while to get into the side. He’s a brilliant passer of the ball. He took his goal very well with a calm finish in the bottom corner.

‘He was feeling a little bit sore, so taking him off was just precautionary.

‘I was also delighted Luke got his goal. That should give him a boost in confidence.’

Oxlade-Chamberlain congratulates McCowan after he scored to make it three for Celtic

McCowan faced criticism after Celtic’s Champions League collapse against LASK and his only previous start this season saw him taken off at half-time in a home defeat by Rangers.

O’Neill said: ‘I thought he did really well, also playing the full game given it has been some considerable time since he has done that.

‘He got the ball early on and played it almost blindly and it was intercepted and I thought, “oh, gosh, here we go”. But he roared back, took his goal well and I am really pleased for him. He is a real genuine lad.

‘It has been tough for him. In the game against Rangers, he was thrown into a position, and it didn’t start well for him in the match. I think he felt it was deja vu for him in terms of the game at the back end of last season too. That will be good for him.’

The Celtic manager also introduced 19-year-old former PSV Eindhoven midfielder Joel van den Berg for a debut in the second half.

‘I thought he did very well,’ said O’Neill. ‘He’s coming on after an injury which kept him out for some time.

‘I am pleased there is a bit of competition for places now.’

The veteran midfielder celebrates his strike that opened the scoring against St Mirren

St Mirren manager Craig McLeish felt Celtic were clinical in his team’s heavy defeat in Glasgow.

‘It’s a really sore one with the way the scoreline ended up,’ said McLeish.

‘I thought we started the game quite well and then that flurry of goals can happen here when you’re playing against such a strong team. The difference was the quality in our box compared to theirs.

‘They are just so clinical, and they get into those good areas and they punish you.

‘I felt we got into some similar areas throughout the game. We didn’t give up, we didn’t move away from what we were trying to do, but we were just really lacking that final bit.’
